Koh Samui is warm all year, with daytime highs of 29–33 °C and a sea temperature of 28–30 °C. The driest, calmest months are February to April. The rain comes with the north-east monsoon from October to December and peaks in November (about 445 mm over 16 rain days), which is the opposite of Phuket. Boat trips run most of the year, but Ang Thong Marine Park closes every year from 1 November to 15 December.

Good to know: Ang Thong Marine Park is closed every year from 1 November to 15 December. Season reopens 16 December. Book now for later dates. Pig Island tours (from 1,450 THB) run on any date, and the Koh Tao day trip runs when the sea allows.

Will my boat trip run? How we decide

Most days of the year, yes. Samui's boat season is long because the island is sheltered from the south-west monsoon that stops boats on the Andaman coast from May to October. The days we lose are mostly from October to January, when strong north-east winds can make the open water unsafe.

  • Who decides: the boat operator and captain make the call on the morning of the trip, based on the latest wind and wave forecasts and any Thai Meteorological Department warnings. We do not run a trip just because it is booked.
  • What happens if it is cancelled: we contact you by WhatsApp or email, and you choose a full refund or a new date. This applies to every tour we sell.
  • What happens if it is choppy but safe: the trip runs. Take seasickness tablets 30–60 minutes before departure, sit at the back of a speedboat, and keep your eyes on the horizon.
  • Crossing times differ: Pig Island boats from Thong Krut take about 30 minutes each way, against roughly 1 h 30 or more to Koh Tao, so a short trip is the better bet when the forecast is mixed.

If you only have one possible boat day, book it early in your stay so there is time to move it if the weather turns. Our normal cancellation rules (full refund 48 hours or more before departure; for Ang Thong, no refund under 48 hours) apply only when you cancel; a weather cancellation by us is always refundable.

The pattern is clear even if exact figures vary: February is the driest month, November the wettest, and the sea never drops below about 28 °C. Nights rarely fall below 24 °C, so there is no "cool season" in the European sense.

Month by month in detail

January

The monsoon's tail: about 127 mm of rain over 8 days, with the occasional windy spell and swell on the east coast. Highs of 29 °C make it one of the most comfortable months. The New Year crowds leave after the first week, and Ang Thong is open. The Full Moon Party falls on 22 January 2027.

February

The best month for most travellers: about 64 mm of rain over just 4 days, the calmest sea of the year and a steady breeze. Book Ang Thong, Koh Tao and Pig Island with confidence. Chinese New Year falls on 6 February 2027, with lion dances in Maenam and Nathon, and Makha Bucha on 21 February brings a one-day stop on alcohol sales in shops.

March

Dry, sunny and calm, with only about 5 rain days and the sea warming to 29 °C. Visibility for snorkelling and diving improves towards April. Hotel prices start to ease after the February peak.

April

The hottest month, with highs of 32 °C and the sea at 30 °C. The water is at its clearest for diving. Songkran (13–15 April 2027) turns Chaweng Beach Road into a water fight, with events usually starting on 12 April; book rooms early.

May

The hottest days of the year (highs of 33 °C) and the first short afternoon showers, about 11 rain days in all. The sea stays calm. The Samui Regatta runs on Chaweng from 22 to 29 May 2027. Prices are low before the summer holidays.

June

Hot and mostly sunny, with brief showers. While Phuket and Krabi are in monsoon, Samui is sheltered and the boats run normally. One of the best-value months for a beach holiday.

July

Similar to June but busier, as European school holidays begin. Expect about 11 short rain days and calm water. Book boat trips a few days ahead.

August

Calm seas on most days and about 102 mm of rain. Peak summer crowds and prices. A good month for families combining Samui with Koh Phangan and Koh Tao.

September

Quieter and cheaper as the holidays end, with mixed sun and showers and the sea still at 29 °C. Diving remains good. The last reliable month before the monsoon.

October

The north-east monsoon arrives: about 295 mm over 16 days, with heavy bursts and rougher seas. It is the last month to visit Ang Thong before the closure. Hotels cut prices and waterfalls start to fill.

November

The wettest month, with about 445 mm over 16 days, surf and red flags on Chaweng and Lamai, and Ang Thong closed. Pig Island tours run on any date, weather permitting. On 24 November 2026 the Full Moon Party and Loy Krathong fall on the same night.

December

Rain eases through the month (about 263 mm over 12 days), Ang Thong reopens on 16 December and the island fills up for Christmas and New Year. Full Moon Parties fall on 24 and 31 December 2026. Book flights and rooms early for the last two weeks.

Weather around the island

Samui is small enough that the rain is broadly the same everywhere, but the wind and sea are not. In the north-east monsoon (October to December) the wind blows onshore on the east coast, so Chaweng, Chaweng Noi and Lamai get the biggest surf, the most red-flag days and the strongest rip currents. The west coast (Lipa Noi, Taling Ngam, Nathon) lies on the far side of the island from that wind. The north coast (Maenam, Bophut, Bang Rak) faces Koh Phangan across a narrow channel, and Choeng Mon sits in a sheltered bay in the north-east.

The interior hills rise to 635 m at Khao Pom, and showers often linger over them, so hill roads and villa driveways can stay wet after the beach has dried. Take care on Route 4170 in the south-west and on steep concrete villa roads after rain. From May to September the wind comes from the south-west, across the mainland, and the sea around the island is calm on most days.

The three seasons

Dry season: January to April

This is Samui's best weather. February has only about 64 mm of rain over 4 rain days, the sea is at its calmest from February to April, and visibility for snorkelling is at its best. January can still bring the tail of the monsoon, with a few windy days and the occasional storm early in the month. April is the hottest month (32 °C highs, 30 °C sea) and also brings Songkran on 13–15 April. Rooms are at their dearest from mid-December to February, so book early.

Hot season with short showers: May to September

While Phuket and Krabi sit in the south-west monsoon, Samui is largely sheltered by the mainland mountains. Expect 10–11 rain days a month, but most are short afternoon showers followed by sunshine. Highs of 32–33 °C and humidity make midday heavy going, so plan beach time for mornings and late afternoons. The sea is calm on most days, which makes this a good time for Ang Thong, Pig Island and Koh Tao. July and August are busy with European school holidays.

North-east monsoon: October to December

From October the wind swings to the north-east and brings the year's rain. October averages about 295 mm, November about 445 mm and December about 263 mm. The rain often arrives in long, heavy bursts, but it does not rain all day every day: with 16 rain days in November, roughly half the month stays dry. The east coast takes the full force of the wind, with surf, red flags and rip currents on Chaweng and Lamai. Low-lying roads can flood after heavy downpours. Ang Thong closes from 1 November to 15 December. In return, the island is green, waterfalls are full and hotel prices are at their lowest before the Christmas peak. If you are coming then, read Koh Samui in November.

Samui vs Phuket and Krabi: opposite seasons

Thailand's two coasts have their rains at different times. The Andaman side (Phuket, Krabi, Koh Lanta, Khao Lak) gets the south-west monsoon from about May to October. The Gulf side (Samui, Phangan, Tao) gets the north-east monsoon from about October to December. That makes Samui a good choice in summer, when Phuket is wet.

January to April is good on both coasts, which is why many travellers combine them; Bangkok Airways flies Phuket–Samui about 7–8 times a day, and the overland route is covered in Phuket and Krabi to Koh Samui.

Storms and typhoons

Full typhoons are rare in the southern Gulf of Thailand, but tropical storms and depressions do pass, most often between late October and January. The most serious recent example was Tropical Storm Pabuk, which crossed the southern Gulf in early January 2019: ferries to Samui, Phangan and Tao were suspended, marine national parks including Ang Thong were closed for several days, and flights were disrupted. Most monsoon seasons bring no named storm at all, just periods of strong wind and heavy rain.

Strong north-east winds can also arrive outside the monsoon. On 19 February 2026, for example, red flags went up along Chaweng and Lamai as 1–2 m waves pounded the east coast and swimming was banned. These "cold surges" from the north usually last one to three days.

How warnings work: the Thai Meteorological Department issues weather and marine warnings for the Gulf, and ferry operators and the national parks suspend services when they apply. When a warning is in force, expect ferries and boat tours to be suspended. Keep your phone charged, follow your hotel's advice and don't swim when flags are red.

Sea, waves and tides

Sea conditions

The sea is calmest from February to April and on most days from May to September. From October to January, strong north-east winds can push 1–2 m waves onto the east coast. Our sea conditions page shows live wave height, wind and a simple calm, choppy or rough verdict.

Tides today

Samui's north and west coasts (Maenam, Bophut, Bang Por, Lipa Noi, Taling Ngam) are shallow and tidal: at low tide you may walk 50 m or more over sand and rock before the water is deep enough to swim. Check the tide before you go:

The full tide tables are on Koh Samui tides.

Ferries in bad weather

Ferries to Koh Phangan and Koh Tao run on choppier water from October to December and can be cancelled when strong north-east winds blow. If you have a flight to catch from Samui, don't plan a Koh Tao return on the same day in monsoon season. Route details: Koh Samui to Koh Phangan, Koh Samui to Koh Tao.

How the weather affects tours and ferries

  • Ang Thong Marine Park closes every year from 1 November to 15 December for the monsoon and reef recovery, and can also close at short notice during storms. Our Ang Thong speedboat tour (1,800 THB, park fee 300 THB cash) books from 16 December.
  • Pig Island trips leave from Thong Krut on the south-west coast and are bookable on any date. The Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB) is our go-to trip from November to mid-December, weather permitting.
  • Koh Tao and Koh Nang Yuan is a long open-water run. The Koh Tao day trip (2,200 THB) runs all year but is the trip most often moved for weather from October to January.
  • Full Moon Party boats run on party nights subject to safe seas. If the crossing is unsafe, you get a full refund or a new date.
  • Outdoor markets such as Fisherman's Village Walking Street often thin out in heavy rain in November and December.
  • Waterfalls are best after rain but can be slippery and fast-flowing; don't climb Na Muang 2 in a downpour.

Hotel pickup for tours is included from most areas of Koh Samui; Nathon, Lipa Noi, Taling Ngam, Bang Kao and Thong Krut (and other remote areas) add 400 THB per person, return. See every trip on Koh Samui tours.

Heat, sun and health

Samui's heat is steady rather than extreme, but it catches people out because nights stay at 24–26 °C and the humidity is high all year. April and May, with highs of 32–33 °C, are the hardest months for walking and sightseeing. Plan temples, viewpoints and waterfalls for the morning, spend 12:00–15:00 in the shade or the sea, and drink more water than you think you need; bottled water is sold at every 7-Eleven.

The sun is strong all year at 9.5° north. Use a high-factor, reef-safe sunscreen, reapply after swimming, and wear a rash vest on snorkelling trips, where backs burn fastest. On boat days the breeze hides the burn until evening.

Mosquitoes are worst after rain, at dawn and at dusk. Dengue fever is present in Thailand all year and peaks in rainy periods, so use repellent and cover up in the evening, especially from October to December. If you develop a high fever after your trip, tell your doctor you have been in Thailand. Private hospitals in Chaweng and Bophut treat visitors around the clock; see hospitals and clinics.

Driving in the rain

Most scooter crashes on Samui happen on wet roads. After heavy rain, the hill roads and the south-west connector (Route 4170) are slippery, painted road markings become like ice, and low-lying stretches of the ring road can flood in the October–December monsoon. Sand washed onto bends is another hazard.

  • If it is pouring, wait it out in a café: outside the monsoon, showers are usually short, and even in November there are dry spells between bursts of rain.
  • Avoid steep concrete villa roads on a scooter when wet; take a taxi or Grab instead.
  • Don't ride through flooded sections; water hides potholes and drains.
  • Wear a helmet (fines up to 2,000 THB) and carry an International Driving Permit that covers motorcycles.

More on Koh Samui roads and getting around.

What to pack for each season

January to April

  • Reef-safe sunscreen (SPF 50), a hat and sunglasses: the UV index is high all day.
  • Light cotton or linen clothes, a cover-up for temples (shoulders and knees covered).
  • Water shoes for stony beaches such as north Lamai, Bang Por and Coral Cove.
  • A light layer for air-conditioned buses, boats and the airport.

May to September

  • Everything above, plus a compact umbrella for afternoon showers.
  • Insect repellent with DEET or picaridin, especially at dusk; dengue is present in Thailand all year and peaks in rainy periods.
  • Seasickness tablets if you are prone to it; the sea is mostly calm but swells happen.

October to December

  • A proper rain jacket or poncho, quick-dry clothes and sandals that grip on wet tiles.
  • A dry bag for phones and passports on boats and scooters.
  • Insect repellent: mosquitoes are at their worst after rain.
  • Indoor plans for heavy-rain days: spa, cooking class, Central Samui mall, Muay Thai nights.
